solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Offensive person's laugh taken in good part

indicators.note: a good part of a phrase is most of it, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone takes a mocking laugh at their expense in good humour rather than being offended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in good part' reads as the idiom for not taking offence; split it, and 'in good part' points to letters sitting within 'person's laugh taken'.
explanation.definitionFit: An offensive, as a noun, is a military attack, and an onslaught is a fierce assault of that kind.

clue.text: Stones hit ought to be turned up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: to slap is to hit
ought, like nought, can mean zero, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone thinks the stones they struck should be flipped over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ought' is an old variant of 'aught' used for nought, so it gives O, not a sense of obligation.
explanation.definitionFit: Opals are precious gemstones, and jewellers commonly call gems stones.

clue.text: Finally get even light on Mozart manuscripts?

parts.note: a bird that lights on a branch settles there
Mozart's handwritten music is old written scores

explanation.surface: A scholar hopes at last to shed light on Mozart's manuscripts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light on' looks like illumination but means to land upon; the question mark flags that old scores is a whimsical description of Mozart's papers.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle old scores is the idiom for taking revenge for past wrongs, finally evening things up.

clue.text: Remove unrealistic summary

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a verb, to take out or extract
second meaning: an adjective, as in art that does not depict things realistically
third meaning: a noun, the brief summary at the head of a paper

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate meanings of one word sit side by side, each a different part of speech, so the clue reads like a nonsense phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb for extracting, an adjective for non-representational art, and a noun for an academic paper's précis.

clue.text: Good sport suppressing a yawn

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold something down and keep it in, so one part encloses another

parts.note: G is the usual abbreviation for good
PE is physical education, school sport
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sporting fellow politely stifles a yawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good sport' reads as a friendly person; split it into two abbreviations, and that pair encloses the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A gape is a wide opening of the mouth, which is exactly what a yawn involves.

clue.text: Waltzers keep this prime title when dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and step into new positions

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Champion ballroom waltzers retain their top title whenever they perform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' is meant in the musical sense of keeping time, not retaining a trophy.
explanation.definitionFit: A waltz is in three beats to the bar, a metre musicians call three-four or triple time.

clue.text: Like an angel taking her away to a higher power

indicators.note: taking something off removes it from the whole
what is sent away no longer remains in the word

parts.note: a cherub is a type of angel
taken as written

explanation.surface: An angel carries a woman off to heaven and God.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A higher power' suggests God, but it is mathematical: raised to the third power.
explanation.definitionFit: Cubic describes a quantity raised to the power of three, higher than squared.

clue.text: Mark of intelligence in part of crossword coterie

indicators.note: one thing placed within another ends up surrounded by it

parts.note: each entry in a crossword has a clue
an IQ score measures intelligence

explanation.surface: Clever solvers form an exclusive crossword circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' is a score, as in an intelligence quotient score.
explanation.definitionFit: A coterie is a small exclusive group of people, the same thing as a clique.

clue.text: They let you construct bridges until PM rages about one

indicators.note: to go about something is to surround it
something raging is wild and disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A construction project stalls while the Prime Minister fumes about a single bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: PM is the Prime Minister; here its two letters are simply part of the mixture.
explanation.definitionFit: Planning authorities issue official permissions allowing a structure to be erected, and these are called building permits.

clue.text: It's smoked fish, alien in name

indicators.note: a thing placed in another is surrounded by it

parts.note: to cite is to name, as a source
the gar is a long-snouted fish
ET is the film alien, the extra-terrestrial

explanation.surface: A smoked fish turns out to have an exotic, foreign-sounding name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoked fish' wants to be a kipper; the definition ends at 'smoked', and fish is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarette is a roll of tobacco that people light and inhale, so it is something smoked.

clue.text: Making sterile cities thrilling with paintings

indicators.note: thrilled things are stirred up and agitated, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Filling cities with exciting art might be thought to make them less dull and clinical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrilling' looks like an adjective describing the cities but works on the words around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To antisepticise is to treat with antiseptic, killing germs and rendering something free of infection.

clue.text: Close pet, nearly shot

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to be in a pet is to be in a sulk
to have a shot is to have a try

explanation.surface: A beloved animal was almost shot at close range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' is the old word for a fit of peevishness, and 'close' is said of weather, not distance.
explanation.definitionFit: Close weather is hot, humid and oppressive, which is just what sultry weather is.

clue.text: Lake creator's imported fish

indicators.note: what is imported is brought inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a founder creates an institution; the 's stands for has
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: The person who made a lake has stocked it with fish brought in from elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creator's' is creator has, and what the founder has taken in is the lake letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A flounder is a flatfish found in European coastal waters and estuaries.

clue.text: Court medic feeding Queen a fish

parts.note: QU is an abbreviation for queen

indicators.note: food goes into a mouth, so one piece is put inside the rest

parts.note: to angle is to fish with rod and line
Dr, doctor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A royal physician serves the Queen a fish dish at court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' is a verb here, and 'Court' is a courtyard, not a royal household.
explanation.definitionFit: A quadrangle is a square courtyard enclosed by buildings, as in an Oxford college, also called a court.

clue.text: Cooked up risotto to cover cold meat

indicators.note: a cover goes all around, so one piece sits inside another
cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A chef makes risotto and spoons it over sliced cold meats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold meat' looks like the definition, but cold supplies a letter and only 'meat' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosciutto is Italian dry-cured ham, usually served thinly sliced as a cold cut.

clue.text: Such moving events may call for a few drinks

definitions.text: Such moving events may call for a few drinks

parts.note: surface reading: emotional occasions, like funerals or weddings, that leave people needing a stiff drink

parts.words: may call for a few drinks
parts.note: setter's reading: outings that literally move from bar to bar, with a drink at each stop

explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' sounds like touching or emotional, but it means the event travels: the group keeps changing venue through the evening.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub crawl is an evening's tour of several bars, stopping for a drink in each one.

clue.text: Fly emperors from the east to the west

indicators.text: from the east to the west
indicators.note: an across entry normally reads west to east, so going the other way runs backwards

parts.note: the Tang dynasty, a line of Chinese emperors

explanation.surface: Emperors flee westward from an eastern land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a verb of escape but is the insect; the emperors are a Chinese dynasty, fitting the eastern setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnat is a small two-winged insect, a kind of fly.

clue.text: Tribal chief's story that goes on further

parts.note: a saga is a long story
more means further, additional

explanation.surface: A tribal leader tells a tale that drags on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', so the definition reads 'tribal chief is'; a saga is also the word for a story that goes on, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagamore was the title of a subordinate chief among Algonquian peoples of north-east America.

clue.text: Wait in the same place endlessly

indicators.note: without ends means both the first and last letters go

parts.note: Latin ibidem, the ibid of footnotes

explanation.surface: Someone is told to stay put and wait without end.
explanation.walkthrough: Ibidem, abbreviated ibid in references, is Latin for in the same place.
explanation.definitionFit: To bide is an old verb meaning to wait or remain, as in biding one's time.

clue.text: Body part very softly separating water

indicators.note: something that separates comes between, so it sits inside the other piece

parts.note: Adam's ale is a jocular term for water
pianissimo, the musical marking for very soft

explanation.surface: A swimmer's limb parts the water gently.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam's ale is an old humorous name for plain water, the only drink the first man had.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adam's apple is the visible bump at the front of the throat formed by the larynx.

clue.text: Mistake overturned without a single observation

indicators.note: turned over in a down entry, the letters run from the bottom up
without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a lapse is a slip or error
I is the numeral one

explanation.surface: A wrong decision is reversed without anyone noticing anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside, so the reversed mistake surrounds the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Espial is the act of spying or catching sight of something, a literary word for watching.

clue.text: Stacks fruit in vehicle

parts.note: ricks are stacks of hay
the haw is the hawthorn's berry

explanation.surface: Someone piles fruit high in a cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a container signal, but the two pieces simply join to form a word that is the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A rickshaw is a light two-wheeled passenger cart pulled by a person or pedalled.

clue.text: Capital, one lost from Bronze Age reconstruction

indicators.note: reconstructing means building again in a fresh form, so the letters are reordered
what is lost from something is no longer part of it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A capital city's Bronze Age reconstruction is missing one piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is removed as the whole word, not as a single I.
explanation.definitionFit: Zagreb is the capital city of Croatia.

clue.text: In Newport, lads brought up really tough

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing up means the letters climb from bottom to top

parts.note: so, as in so good, means really
a tough is a thug, a yob in British slang

explanation.surface: Boys raised in a Welsh port town grow up hard.
explanation.walkthrough: Newport is a city in south Wales, and boyo is Welsh English for a lad; 'tough' is a noun, a yob being a hooligan.
explanation.definitionFit: Boyo is a Welsh dialect word for a boy or young man, so lads as a Welsh speaker would say.

clue.text: Sucker lacking passion and someone to seduce him?

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so these letters are removed

parts.note: a vampire sucks blood
ire is anger, a strong passion

explanation.surface: A gullible man with no ardour needs a woman to lead him on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucker' suggests a dupe, but it is a bloodsucker; and the 'him' is that dupe, so the definition sits naturally in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A vamp is a seductive woman who uses her charms to exploit men, a femme fatale.

clue.text: What ensures voting success? Manipulating voting age!

parts.note: to work something is to manipulate it
the age of majority is when one may vote

explanation.surface: A cynic suggests rigging the voting age is the way to win elections.
explanation.walkthrough: Majority also means legal adulthood, the age at which a citizen may vote, so 'voting age' gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: A working majority is a parliamentary margin large enough for a government to pass its legislation reliably.

clue.text: Fibre one's covered with tar mostly

indicators.note: a covering wraps around, so one piece sits inside the other
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a tar and a salt are both old words for a sailor
one is I, plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A rope's fibre has been largely coated in tar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tar' looks like the black sticky stuff ropes are dipped in, but it means a sailor, as does salt.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a strong plant fibre from an agave, used for rope and matting.

clue.text: Papers retained by lovers of old trains

indicators.note: what is retained by something is held inside it

parts.note: former partners are exes
the press, newspapers collectively

explanation.surface: Railway enthusiasts hoard old documents about vintage trains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lovers of old trains' reads as train buffs, but 'of old' attaches to lovers, meaning former partners.
explanation.definitionFit: Expresses are fast trains making few stops, the plural noun of express.
